title: Instance-Adaptive Online Multicalibration
claim: The current adaptive partition of a prediction interval is equivalent to a tree whose leaves are the active bins.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, double arrow linking interval bar and tree
description: Two panels joined by a double-headed arrow. The left panel, titled 'Active partition B_t', shows a horizontal bar on [0,1] shaded light blue and split into five unequal intervals. The split points are marked 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 7/8 and 1. Each interval has a dark blue dot at its midpoint. A caption below says the learner predicts a mixture over the leaf midpoints {r_I : I in B_t}. The right panel, titled 'Corresponding dyadic tree', shows a binary tree. White internal nodes are connected by black lines to light blue leaf nodes. Each leaf is labeled with its interval, such as [0,1/4) or [7/8,1]. The right branch is deeper than the left, so the bin sizes are uneven. A caption says internal nodes have already split and leaves are the current active bins. The figure is black, white and light blue, with a minimal style.
caption: A typical state of the dynamic-bin data structure. The learner predicts using the midpoints of the current leaves, and an interval is reﬁned only after the total mass assigned to it reaches the threshold L/w2
abstract: We study online multicalibration beyond the worst-case. We give a single, efficient algorithm which dynamically interpolates between benign and worst-case sequences by adaptively refining a dyadic grid of prediction values. Its error is controlled by the number of leaves in the refinement tree. Our analysis recovers the known $\widetilde O(T^{2/3})$ worst-case-optimal rate for online multicalibration, while simultaneously automatically adapting to easier instances: in the marginal stochastic setting it obtains a rate of $\widetilde O(\sqrt T)$, and for piecewise-stationary means with $J$ segments its rate is $\widetilde O(\sqrt{JT})$. More generally, the rate depends on a threshold-complexity measure of the predictable mean process relative to the group family. We show that this dependence is tight up to logarithmic factors.
